facts.statement: The genus Devincenzia was described by Kraglievich in 1932.
facts.quote: authority: Kraglievich, 1932

facts.statement: The first fossils attributed to the genus were described in 1931 by Lucas Kraglievich.
facts.quote: The first fossil attributed to the genus, an incomplete tarsometatarsus (lower leg bone) and toe bone, were described in 1931 by Uruguayan naturalist Lucas Kraglievich as coming from a new species of Phorusrhacos, P. pozzi.

facts.statement: The initial specimens were found in the Ituzaingó Formation in southern Argentina.
facts.quote: This specimen was discovered in sediments of the Ituzaingó Formation in Paraná, Río Negro Province in southern Argentina.

facts.statement: Devincenzia was more robust and adapted for ambush hunting than its relatives Phorusrhacos and Titanis.
facts.quote: Like Kelenken, Devincenzia was more robust and graviportal (adapted for ambush hunting) than the other phorusrhacines Phorusrhacos and Titanis.

facts.statement: Devincenzia was carnivorous and possibly a scavenger.
facts.quote: Devincenzia was carnivorous, though may have been a scavenger.

facts.statement: The largest possible specimen may have been 2 meters tall and weighed between 200 and 500 kg.
facts.quote: The largest possible specimen may have measured 2 m tall and weighed 200-500 kg.

facts.statement: The Uruguayan specimen likely originates from the Arroyo Roman, dating to the Miocene or Oligocene.
facts.quote: It likely comes from the Arroyo Roman, which bears localities dating to the Miocene and Oligocene.

facts.statement: The first fossils were cataloged at the MACN as MACN PV 6554 and MACN PV 6681.
facts.quote: Fossils of Devincenzia were first described in 1931 by Uruguayan paleontologist Lucas Kraglievich and included a large, incomplete tarsometatarsus and an associated pedal phalanx (toe bone), which were cataloged at the Bernardino Rivadavia Natural Sciences Argentine Museum (MACN) as MACN PV 6554 and MACN PV 6681 respectfully.

facts.statement: The remains were collected from the Ituzaingó Formation in Entre Ríos Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: These remains were collected from layers of the Ituzaingó Formation in Paraná in Entre Ríos Province, Argentina, which derives from the "Mesopotamian" (now called the Huayquerian) SALMA (South American Land Mammal Ages; a series of mammalian fauna-based geologic ages) of the Late Miocene.

facts.statement: A tarsometatarsus deposited at the National Museum of Natural History in France was described in 1932.
facts.quote: In 1932, Kraglievich described an isolated tarsometatarsus, deposited at the National Museum of Natural History, France under MNHN-189, that had been unearthed in an unknown locality in Uruguay.

facts.statement: Kraglievich originally placed Devincenzia in its own family, Devincenziidae, within Stereornithes.
facts.quote: Kraglievich assigned Devincenzia in its own family, the Devincenziidae, which was placed within Stereornithes (an outdated name for Phorusrhacidae).

facts.statement: An incomplete skull and two pedal phalanges were unearthed in 1933 near Lake Epecuén in Buenos Aires Province.
facts.quote: In late August and early September of 1933, fossil preparator Antonio Castro unearthed an incomplete skull and two pedal phalanges of a large phorusrhacid outside of a lagoon in Lake Epecuén in the southern Pampas of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina.

facts.statement: Angelo Cabrera described these remains as Onactornis depressus in 1939.
facts.quote: In 1939, Argentine paleontologist Angelo Cabrera scientifically described the skull and pedal phalanges, which were deposited at the Museo de La Plata under MLP 37-III-7-8, as belonging to a new genus and species of bird, Onactornis depressus.

facts.statement: Whether Onactornis and Devincenzia are synonyms remains a subject of debate.
facts.quote: This has seen support from some other authors, but is still a subject of debate.

facts.statement: In 2008, Noriega and Agnolín tentatively assigned two vertebrae to D. pozzi.
facts.quote: In 2008, Argentine paleontologists Jorge Noriega and Agnolín tentatively assigned two, giant phorusrhacid vertebrae, one a cervical (neck) vertebra and the other a dorsal (back) vertebra, to D. pozzi.

facts.statement: Devincenzia is larger and bulkier than Titanis and Phorusrhacos.
facts.quote: Overall, Devincenzia is larger and bulkier than its relatives Titanis and Phorusrhacos, representing one of the largest members of the family.

facts.statement: The complete skull of Devincenzia was approximately 64.5 cm long, similar in size to Phorusrhacos but shorter than Kelenken.
facts.quote: When complete, it was around 64.5 cm long and about the size of Phorusrhacos', but shorter than Kelenken's.

facts.statement: The preserved skull specimen was flattened by taphonomic processes and includes extensive plaster reconstruction.
facts.quote: The skull was flattened from top to bottom by taphonomy and the specimen contains extensive plaster reconstruction.

facts.statement: Unlike other phorusrhacids, the fossae in Devincenzia are bordered by large bony ridges.
facts.quote: Unlike in other phorusrhacids, these fossae are bordered by large bony ridges.

facts.statement: The skull's height-to-width ratio in Devincenzia is about 39%, compared to 47% in Phorusrhacos and 48% in Psilopterus.
facts.quote: The ratio from height to width is about 39%, while in Phorusrhacos it is 47% and in Psilopterus it is 48%.

facts.statement: The jugal bone in Devincenzia is robust, convex, and sigmoid-shaped, contrasting with the shallow jugals of Psilopterus and Tolmodus.
facts.quote: MLP 37-III-7-8 preserves the entire jugal, which is markedly robust, convex, and sigmoid-shaped, unlike the shallow jugals of Psilopterus and Tolmodus.

facts.statement: The tarsometatarsus anatomy of Devincenzia is intermediate between lithe phorusrhacines and robust brontornithines.
facts.quote: The tarsometatarsus' anatomy is intermediary between the lithe phorusrhacines and the robust brontornithines (physornithines).

facts.statement: The holotype of D. gallinali is less robust because it is not fully mature, as shown by its cortical bone.
facts.quote: However, the holotype of D. gallinali is not fully mature as demonstrated by its cortical bone, and is therefore less robust.

facts.statement: A complete tibiotarsus from the Early Pleistocene Raigón Formation of southern Uruguay was described by Claude Tambussi and colleagues in 1999.
facts.quote: A complete tibiotarsus of a phorusrhacine from the Early Pleistocene Raigón Formation of southern Uruguay was described by Argentine paleontologist Claude Tambussi and colleagues in 1999.

facts.statement: Brazilian paleontologists Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling tentatively assigned the Raigón Formation tibiotarsus to Devincenzia in 2003.
facts.quote: Brazilian paleontologists Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling tentatively assigned the specimen to Devincenzia in 2003.

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling suggested phorusrhacids were flightless based on wing-to-body mass proportions, noting that wing size was more reduced in larger members.
facts.quote: Alvarenga and Höfling suggested that phorusrhacids were flightless, as evidenced by the proportional size of their wings and body mass, and wing-size was more reduced in larger members of the group.

facts.statement: Large lacrimal bone expansions likely protected eyes from the sun and enabled keen eyesight, indicating hunting in open, sunlit areas rather than shaded forests.
facts.quote: The large expansions above the eyes formed by the lacrimal bones (similar to what is seen in modern hawks) would have protected the eyes against the sun, and enabled keen eyesight, which indicates they hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas, and not shaded forests.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested future studies should examine if phorusrhacids used beaks and claws against well-armored mammals like armadillos and glyptodonts.
facts.quote: They also suggested future studies could examine whether they could have used their beaks and claws against well-armored mammals such as armadillos and glyptodonts.

facts.statement: A phorusrhacine tibiotarsus from the Early Pleistocene Raigón Formation of southern Uruguay was described in 1999.
facts.quote: A complete tibiotarsus of a phorusrhacine from the Early Pleistocene Raigón Formation of southern Uruguay was described by Argentine paleontologist Claude Tambussi and colleagues in 1999.

facts.statement: A phorusrhacine from the La Venta Formation of Colombia is larger than the D. pozzi tibiotarsus.
facts.quote: However, it is about 18% smaller than MT-0200, an unnamed phorusrhacine from the La Venta Formation of Colombia.

facts.statement: The discovery of Kelenken challenged the traditional view that larger phorusrhacids were less agile and adapted for running.
facts.quote: According to Argentine paleontologists Luis Chiappe and Sara Bertelli in a 2006 article, the discovery of Kelenken shed doubt on the traditional idea that the size and agility of phorusrhacids correlated, with the larger members of the group being more bulky and less adapted for running.

facts.statement: Researchers assumed the neck adaptations found in Andalgalornis would also apply to other large phorusrhacids like Devincenzia.
facts.quote: the researchers assumed the same would be true for other large, big-headed phorusrhacids like Devincenzia.

facts.statement: Studies suggest that while both skull types handled prey similarly, the rigid skulls of the "Terror Bird" type were an adaptation for handling larger prey.
facts.quote: Despite the differences, studies have shown the two types handled prey similarly, while the more rigid skulls and resulting larger bite force of the "Terror Bird" type would have been an adaptation to handling larger prey.

facts.statement: Kraglievich described Devincenzia in 1932 as the sole member of the distinct family Devincenziidae.
facts.quote: In his description of Devincenzia, Kraglievich (1932) dubbed Devincenziidae, a distinct family that included just Devincenzia.

facts.statement: Recent studies consider Psilopteridae and Devincenziidae synonymous with Phorusrhacidae, but Opisthodactylidae and Brontornithidae contain genera not included in Phorusrhacidae.
facts.quote: While Psilopteridae and Devincenziidae are now considered synonymous with Phorusrhacidae, Opisthodactylidae and Brontornithidae contained genera not included in Phorusrhacidae according to recent studies.

facts.statement: Brodkorb corrected the spelling of the family name from Phororhacidae to Phorusrhacidae in 1967.
facts.quote: It was not until Brodkorb (1967) that Phororhacidae was corrected to Phorusrhacidae in literature.

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling published a 2003 revision of the family recognizing six subfamilies, including Phorusrhacinae.
facts.quote: In 2003, Brazilian paleontologists Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling published a revision of the family in which they recognized six subfamilies, including Phorusrhacinae, and defined each one.

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling included Devincenzia in the subfamily Phorusrhacinae alongside Phorusrhacos and Titanis.
facts.quote: Devincenzia was included in Phorusrhacinae along with Phorusrhacos and Titanis.

facts.statement: A 2015 analysis by Degrange united Devincenzia with Kelenken outside a polytomy of other subfamilies.
facts.quote: A later phylogenetic analysis by Degrange and colleagues (2015) found Phorusrhacidae to include Mesembrironithinae and Psilopterinae as distinct, while Patagornithinae, Phorusrhacinae, and Physornithinae is in polytomy (topology 2). Here, Devincenzia was united with Kelenken outside of the polytomy including patagornithines, phorusrhacines, and physornithines.

facts.statement: Kraglievich first used the name Phorusrhacinae in 1932 to include Phorusrhacos longissimus, Devincenzia gallinali, their descendants, and their most recent common ancestor.
facts.quote: The name "Phorusrhacinae" was first used by Kraglievich (1932) and defined as including Phorusrhacos longissimus, Devincenzia gallinali, their descendents, and their most recent common ancestor.

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling limited the subfamily Phorusrhacinae to Phorusrhacos, Devincenzia, Kelenken, and Titanis in 2003.
facts.quote: Alvarenga and Höfling (2003) limited Phorusrhacinae to Phorusrhacos, Devincenzia, Kelenken, and Titanis.

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling defined Phorusrhacinae members by gigantic build, lithe traits, and a tarsometatarsus over 60% the length of the tibiotarsus.
facts.quote: They defined (the traits taxa have to be considered members) Phorusrhacinae by the presence of an overall size and gigantic build, more lithe traits than Brontornithinae (a clade which may not be phorusrhacid), and a relatively elongated and slender tarsometatarsus, which is over 60% of the length of the tibiotarsus.

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling considered a mandibular symphysis over twice as long as its base width a defining characteristic of Phorusrhacinae.
facts.quote: Furthermore, a relatively long, narrow, and relatively dorsoventrally (top-bottom) short mandibular symphysis (the area where both mandibulae (lower jaws) meet) which measures over twice as long as the width of the base was considered a defining characteristic too.

facts.statement: Agnolín expanded the subfamily Phorusrhacinae in 2009 to include Physornithini alongside other genera.
facts.quote: Agnolín (2009) expanded Phorusrhacinae to include Phorusrhacos, Andalgalornis, Devincenzia, Kelenken, Titanis, and the tribe Physornithini, which is composed of Physornis and Paraphysornis.

facts.statement: Agnolín distinguished Phorusrhacinae by a tall, robust postorbital process and a subrectangular antorbital fenestra.
facts.quote: He stated the group was distinguished from other phorusrhacids by the presence of a tall, robust postorbital process (an extension on the quadrate that interlocked with the postorbital bone) and a subrectangular antorbital fenestra (a gap in the skull in front of the orbit).

facts.statement: LaBarge, Organ, and Gardner suggested that the close relationship between Kelenken and Devincenzia found in their 2024 analysis may result from parallel evolution of robust traits.
facts.quote: Although their analysis found Kelenken and Devincenzia as closer to Physornithi, La Barge, Organ, and Gardner (2024) stated that this may be a result of parallel evolution of robust traits, as Phorusrhacos was relatively gracile and cursorial.

facts.statement: LaBarge, Organ, and Gardner continued to include Devincenzia and Kelenken in the subfamily Phorusrhacinae despite their phylogenetic results.
facts.quote: This led them to continue to include Devincenzia and Kelenken in the subfamily despite the results.

facts.statement: Phorusrhacids dispersed into North America during the Great American Biotic Interchange approximately 3 million years ago.
facts.quote: They dispersed into North America during the Great American Biotic Interchange (~3 Ma).

facts.statement: Assignments of remains from Africa, Europe, and the Paleocene of Brazil to Phorusrhacidae or as related to seriemas remain controversial.
facts.quote: Some remains from Africa and Europe and the Paleocene of Brazil have been assigned to this clade or identified as phylogenetically related to the extant South American seriemas, but these assignments remain controversial.

facts.statement: Agnolín's stance on Phorusrhacinae composition was backed by a phylogenetic analysis finding Kelenken and Devincenzia as sister taxa.
facts.quote: Agnolín's stance was backed by a phylogenetic analysis, which found Kelenken and Devincenzia to be sister taxa.

facts.statement: The Ituzaingó Formation dates to the Late Miocene, a time of high biodiversity in South America.
facts.quote: The strata of the Ituzaingó Formation date to the Late Miocene, a period in which animal biodiversity boomed in South America

facts.statement: The Ituzaingó Formation represents deposits from the beaches of the Paranese Sea, indicating a subtropical environment.
facts.quote: The Ituzaingó Formation's deposits are from the beaches of the Paranese Sea, transforming the environment into a subtropical one

facts.statement: The environment included common bamboos and palms alongside coastal, riverine, tropical, and savanna habitats.
facts.quote: Bamboos, coconut palms, and other palms were very common. Its flora also included savannas in addition to the coastal, riverine, and tropical regions.

facts.statement: Fossils of Onactornis depressus, considered a possible synonym of Devincenzia, were discovered in the Cerro Azul Formation.
facts.quote: Fossils of Onactornis depressus, a possible synonym of Devincenzia, were found in strata of the Cerro Azul Formation.

facts.statement: The Cerro Azul Formation dates between 10 and 5.7 million years ago based on its fauna and stratigraphy.
facts.quote: Based on its fauna and stratigraphy, the Cerro Azul Formation dates to between 10 and 5.8-5.7 million years old.

facts.statement: During the Miocene, the Cerro Azul region had a neotropical climate supporting animals adapted to warm conditions.
facts.quote: In the Miocene, the Cerro Azul had a neotropical climate and harbored animals adapted for warm climates like frogs, turtles, and snakes.
